title: Fitting a Cat6 data socket on a wall plate
subtitle: Terminate a Cat6 network cable into a keystone module and fit a single or double wall plate for a wired network point
excerpt: How to fit a Cat6 network data socket. Covers stripping the cable, terminating the four pairs into a keystone module using T568B colour coding, and fitting the module into a wall plate on a back box.
sourceNotes: TIA-568C standard for structured cabling (open access). UK wiring practice for data installations. Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: Category 6 unshielded twisted-pair (UTP) data cable. Contains four twisted pairs of 23 AWG conductors, colour coded in matching pairs: orange/white-orange, green/white-green, blue/white-blue, brown/white-brown. Supports Gigabit Ethernet at up to 100 m. Also compatible with Cat5e wall plates and patch panels.

The common colour sequence for terminating Cat5e and Cat6 cables into RJ45 keystone modules and patch panels in the UK. Order from pin 1: white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown. T568A and T568B are both standards; T568B is the more common in domestic and commercial UK installations.

A modular RJ45 jack that terminates individual wire pairs into a punch-down block and snaps into a standard keystone wall plate. The IDC (insulation displacement connector) type punches down eight conductors in one action; no soldering.

, then the module clips into the wall plate. No mains electricity is involved; the data socket is low-voltage signal only.

Strip the outer jacket of the cable by 50 mm using the wire stripper's cable stripper slot or a careful score with the utility knife (do not nick the inner pairs). Untwist each pair. Note the four pairs and their colour code. Keep the untwisted length to no more than 13 mm from the jacket end to maintain the pair twist as close to the termination as possible; Cat6 performance degrades with excessive untwisting.
Punch down into the keystone module

The keystone module has a colour-coded punch-down block; both T568A and T568B labels are usually printed. Press each conductor into the correct slot following the T568B colour order. Use a punch-down tool to seat and trim each conductor in one action. If the module uses a cap (a clip that forces all eight conductors into the IDC contacts simultaneously), lay the conductors into the cap slots in T568B order, seat the cap firmly over the contacts, and clip it into place.

Snap the keystone module into the wall plate. Screw the wall plate to the surface-mounted or flush-mounted back box. Feed the cable into the back box before fitting the plate. Use a flush-mounted steel back box in a plasterboard or masonry wall (chase the cable into the wall or run it in conduit); use a surface-mount PVC back box when surface-running the cable.

Connect a network cable tester between the new wall plate and the other end of the run (the patch panel or router port). A tester lights eight LEDs in order (1 through 8) to confirm each pair is wired correctly and there are no cross-wires. A basic cable tester is available for around five pounds from most electronics retailers. Without a tester, plug a device in and confirm the network connection is live.

attrs.cause: One or more conductors are not punched down correctly, or the wrong colour code was used.
attrs.fix: Unclip the module and re-check the T568B sequence against the module colour labels. Re-punch any conductor that is not fully seated.

attrs.symptom: Connection works but at reduced speed (100 Mbps instead of Gigabit)
attrs.cause: Only two pairs are correctly terminated (100 Mbps uses two pairs; Gigabit uses all four).
attrs.fix: Check that all four pairs are punched down and that none are cross-wired between pairs.
